scenes.name: one operation, deliberately tiny
scenes.visual: One continuous shot on the dark canvas. Top right: a stopwatch icon reading '30 ms' beside a blue token pill 'one token', the callback to the per-token time from earlier. Centre: an 'arithmetic bench' where blue number cards meet an amber operator sign and produce an amber result card, used once for a multiply and once for an add. Bottom right: a tally counter 'operations' that ticks up by exactly one for every operation shown. The heading exists only during b2; from b3 on, only the bench, the word FLOP and the tally remain. The idea the motion makes visible: an operation is one tiny act on two numbers, and the chapter is about to count enormous numbers of them.

beats.say: Earlier you heard that the arithmetic for one token takes about a tenth of a millisecond. Time to check.
beats.show: Top right: the stopwatch '30 ms' and the blue 'one token' pill fade in. On 'a tenth of a millisecond', a small amber tag drops beneath them: 'arithmetic: 0.1 ms?'. On 'Time to check', the '?' pulses and the tally counter appears bottom right: 'operations: 0'.

beats.say: An operation is one piece of arithmetic. One multiplication or one addition, on two numbers. Not a line of code, nor a step of reasoning.
beats.show: Centre top, a white heading writes on: 'one operation = one piece of arithmetic'. On 'one multiplication', blue cards 'input 0.5' and 'weight 0.13' slide together through an amber '×' and produce an amber card '0.065'; the tally ticks to 1. On 'one addition', a blue card 'total 1.2' takes in the 0.065 through an amber '+' and becomes '1.265'; the tally ticks to 2. On 'a line of code' and 'a step of reasoning', grey ghost cards with those labels (a code-brackets icon, a lightbulb icon) drift in at the left, are struck through and fade.

beats.say: Its proper name is a floating-point operation, or flop. Floating point just means numbers with a fractional part, like the weights. Counting them measures a job, the way metres measure distance.
beats.show: The heading fades and the bench dims to 40%. Centre: 'FLoating-point OPeration' writes on with F, L, O and P in amber; the four letters slide together into one large amber word, 'FLOP'. On 'fractional part', the bench's weight card brightens and its '.13' is underlined in amber. On 'metres', a ruler icon appears left of FLOP, with small grey labels under each: '1 metre: distance' and '1 FLOP: work'.

beats.say: A flop is deliberately tiny. Soon one token will cost a hundred and forty billion of exactly these.
beats.show: The ruler and both labels fade; FLOP shrinks to the top left and stays. The camera pushes in on the tally reading '2'. On 'a hundred and forty billion', the tally spins up to '140,000,000,000' and the 'one token' pill slides down from the top right to sit above it.

scenes.name: reading the big numbers
scenes.visual: A table of powers of ten. Left column (x 80 to 280): five blue pills with raised exponents, '10³', '10⁶', '10⁹', '10¹²', '10¹⁵', each with its word name in small grey beneath it ('thousand', 'million', 'billion', 'trillion', 'quadrillion'). To the right, one horizontal lane per row from x=300 to x=1800, 1,500 px. In b1 and b2 each lane holds that row's digit string, starting at x=320; the digit strings fade out at the very start of b3, before any bar grows. In b3 the lanes hold bars, first on an ordinary scale, then morphing to a true logarithmic scale at 100 px per power of ten (300, 600, 900, 1,200, 1,500 px). This is the film's first log scale, so the morph between the two scales is the explanation. Bars are blue until the two that matter turn amber. In b4 an amber sixth row for 10¹¹ slides in between the billion and trillion rows.

beats.say: Numbers that big need a shorthand. Ten to the three is a one followed by three zeros, a thousand. The small raised number, the exponent, counts the zeros.
beats.show: Top row only. On 'ten to the three', the pill '10³' fades in with 'thousand' under it. In its lane, from x=320, the digits type out: a '1', then three zeros dropping in one at a time while the raised 3 pulses once per zero. On 'exponent', a thin white callout points at the raised 3: 'exponent = number of zeros'.

beats.say: Then a million, a billion, a trillion, and ten to the fifteen, a quadrillion, a thousand million million. Each step is a thousand times the last.
beats.show: Rows two to five land on their spoken names: '10⁶', '10⁹', '10¹²', '10¹⁵'. Each digit string is the row above's plus three new zeros, which flash amber as they arrive. On 'a thousand million million', brackets group the 10¹⁵ string as '1 000' 'thousand', '000 000' 'million', '000 000' 'million'. On 'a thousand times the last', small amber '× 1,000' tags appear in the left margin between neighbouring rows. At the end of the beat the callout, the brackets and the margin tags fade.

beats.say: On an ordinary scale, the quadrillion fills the width and the rest vanish. Let each bar count zeros instead, a logarithmic scale, and all five fit.
beats.show: The digit strings fade out first. A grey axis title appears under the lanes: 'ordinary scale'. Blue bars grow: the 10¹⁵ bar sweeps to the full 1,500 px; the 10¹² bar is a 1.5 px hairline; the three rows above stay empty, with one grey bracket spanning all three: 'too small to draw'. On 'count zeros', the bracket fades, the axis title changes to 'log scale: length = zeros', and the bars morph to 300, 600, 900, 1,200 and 1,500 px, an even staircase. Light tick marks sit every 300 px; only the first gap is labelled '× 1,000'. Each bar shows its zero count inside it in white: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.

beats.say: The whole argument compares two of these. A chip does about ten to the fifteen operations a second, and a token needs about ten to the eleven. Four powers of ten apart, so each second, the chip could do ten thousand tokens' worth.
beats.show: The thousand, million and billion rows dim to 30%, and the axis title and the '× 1,000' gap label fade. On 'ten to the fifteen operations a second', the 10¹⁵ bar turns amber with the tag 'a chip, per second'. On 'ten to the eleven', a new amber row slides in between billion and trillion: pill '10¹¹', name 'hundred billion', bar 1,100 px, tag 'one token'. On 'four powers of ten', a white bracket spans from the end of the 10¹¹ bar at 1,100 px to the end of the 10¹⁵ bar at 1,500 px, labelled '4 powers of ten'. On 'ten thousand tokens' worth', the label changes to '× 10,000: tokens' worth per second'.

scenes.name: a count and a rate
scenes.visual: Split screen with a thin vertical divider. Left panel 'A count': an amber stack of tiny operation chips under a counter, a blue token pill on top, and no clock anywhere. Right panel 'A rate': a horizontal pipe carrying amber particles past a stopwatch, with a per-second counter; the constant flow speed stands for the rate. Below the panels the words FLOP and FLOPS appear in b2. A grey sample-sentence card is corrected in b3. At the end the two panel titles fly to the centre and form 'count ÷ rate = seconds', the takeaway. Text discipline: once the words arrive in b2, the panels keep only their titles and counters.

beats.say: Ten to the eleven is a count, how many operations a job needs, with no time in it. Ten to the fifteen a second is a rate, with time built in.
beats.show: The two amber rows from the table, 10¹¹ and 10¹⁵, lift out; their pills fly apart and become the panels' counters. Left: title 'A count', counter '10¹¹ operations', an amber chip stack growing beneath it with the blue 'one token' pill on top, sub-label 'no time in it'; on 'no time in it', a grey stopwatch icon beside the stack is struck through. On 'a rate', right: title 'A rate', counter '10¹⁵ operations / second', a chip icon emitting amber particles along a pipe past a stopwatch whose hand sweeps steadily, sub-label 'time is built in'.

beats.say: Yet they are written almost the same. Flop for the count, flops for the rate, and some add a small letter ess to the count just to make it plural.
beats.show: Both sub-labels dim to 25%, leaving titles and counters. Large white 'FLOP' appears under the left panel and 'FLOPS' under the right. On 'flops for the rate', the final S glows amber with a small caption 'S = per second'. On 'small letter ess', a grey third word, 'FLOPs' with a lower-case s, appears between them with a '?'.

beats.say: Confusing the two is the single most common mistake in this subject, and checking the units catches it.
beats.show: On 'confusing the two', the three words slide together and blur, then snap apart. On 'checking the units', a grey sentence card slides in at the bottom centre: 'this chip does 10¹⁵ FLOP'. A teal magnifier passes over it, a gap glows where '/ second' belongs, the card corrects itself to 'this chip does 10¹⁵ FLOPS', and a teal check appears.

beats.say: Divide a count by a rate, like distance by speed, and you get a time. That one division is the entire calculation ahead.
beats.show: The card and the three words fade, and the panels dim to 25%. The two panel titles lift and fly to the centre, assembling 'count' (amber) '÷' 'rate' (amber) '=' 'time' (white). On 'distance by speed', a small grey line with a car icon appears beneath: '300 km ÷ 100 km/h = 3 h'. On 'entire calculation ahead', the grey line fades, 'time' becomes 'seconds', and the equation enlarges and glows.

scenes.name: the arithmetic adds up to a tenth of a millisecond
scenes.visual: Left third: a chip icon (the compute die of the GPU package) with amber particles pouring through it, labelled with its rate. Right third: a blue token pill with the operation count derived beneath it. Upper centre, in b2 only: a one-millisecond measuring strip. Bottom band from b3: a timeline from 0 to 30 ms, 1,500 px from x=210 to x=1710 (50 px per millisecond), a stopwatch icon at its left end. The idea: the arithmetic for one token is spread thinly across the whole 30 ms in tiny bursts; packed together it is a 5 px block, and the rest of the timeline is something else. The packed block is a share of the time, never a claim that the arithmetic happens first, and its 'packed together' tag travels with it into the later scenes.

beats.say: First, the count. Each token uses all seventy billion weights, each multiplied once and added once. Two operations per weight make a hundred and forty billion, about ten to the eleven.
beats.show: Left third: the chip icon fades in with amber particles streaming through it, label '≈ 10¹⁵ operations / second', small grey tag 'exact spec: next chapter'. Right third: the blue pill 'one token'; below it, the multiply-and-add picture from earlier in miniature: five blue input cards, each with an amber '×' and a blue weight card, arrows into one amber '+'. On 'multiplied once', every '×' flashes; on 'added once', the '+' flashes. An equation builds under it, term by term: '70,000,000,000 weights' (blue) '× 2' (amber) '= 140,000,000,000' (amber). On 'about ten to the eleven', it collapses to '≈ 10¹¹ operations' with a grey tag 'really 1.4 × 10¹¹'.

beats.say: Now divide. A quadrillion a second is a trillion every millisecond. A token needs a tenth of that, so its arithmetic adds up to a tenth of a millisecond.
beats.show: Upper centre: a horizontal strip 1,000 px wide labelled '1 millisecond', split into ten equal ticks, with '10¹² operations' above it; on 'a trillion every millisecond', amber particles from the chip fill the whole strip. On 'a tenth of that', the particles drain away except for exactly one tick, which stays amber, labelled '10¹¹ → 0.1 ms'. The strip measures an amount of time; it is not a clock.

beats.say: Yet each token takes thirty. The arithmetic comes in tiny bursts, spread across all thirty. Squeezed together, it would fill just the first zero point one.
beats.show: The strip shrinks away. Bottom band: the timeline draws on from '0' to '30 ms', the stopwatch at its left. On 'tiny bursts', about twenty amber hairline ticks appear, spaced evenly across the whole 0 to 30 ms, with a grey label 'arithmetic comes in bursts' (the ticks are as thin as the renderer allows; their widths are not to scale). On 'squeezed together', the 'bursts' label fades and the ticks slide left and merge into one 5 px amber block at the start, now to scale, with a grey tag 'all the arithmetic, packed together'.

beats.say: That leaves twenty-nine point nine milliseconds, room for three hundred more tokens' worth. Everything ahead answers one question. Why is that time not free?
beats.show: The rest of the timeline becomes an empty grey outline labelled '29.9 ms'. On 'three hundred more tokens' worth', a counter at its right end runs from 0 to 299 and settles as '≈ 300 more tokens' worth'. On 'one question', the chip and token cards dim and their two numbers fly to the centre to form '10¹¹ ÷ 10¹⁵ = 0.1 ms', subtitled 'two numbers, one division'. On 'not free', the counter fades, the grey part of the timeline pulses once, and a white label lands on it: 'why not free?'.

scenes.name: doing the division slowly, units and all
scenes.visual: Centre left (x 160 to 1100): a large fraction, '10¹¹ operations' over '10¹⁵ operations per second', powers in amber, unit words in white. The powers unfold into rows of small amber '10' tiles, eleven on top and fifteen beneath, which cancel in pairs and leave four underneath: 'subtract the exponents', made visible. Right (x 1200 to 1800): a results ladder builds downward, one line per step: '= 10⁽¹¹⁻¹⁵⁾', '= 10⁻⁴ seconds', '= 0.0001 seconds', '= 0.1 milliseconds'. Then the same fraction is read for its units alone, a grey 'the wrong way' panel replaces the ladder, and everything shrinks into a row of three example cards under a teal banner. One continuous shot; the numbers part and the units part share the same fraction.

beats.say: That division is the whole puzzle, so do it slowly. To divide powers of ten, subtract the exponents. Eleven tens over fifteen tens. Eleven pairs cancel, and four stay on the bottom.
beats.show: Heading: 'dividing powers of ten: subtract the exponents'. The numerator '10¹¹ operations' writes on, the fraction bar draws, then the denominator '10¹⁵ operations per second'. On 'eleven tens', 10¹¹ unfolds into eleven amber '10' tiles joined by '×'; on 'fifteen tens', 10¹⁵ unfolds into fifteen, left-aligned so the first eleven sit directly under the eleven above. On 'eleven pairs cancel', tile pairs strike through together and fade, left to right, with a small counter '11 pairs'. The top row becomes '1'; four amber tiles remain on the bottom, glowing, tagged '4 left, on the bottom'.

beats.say: Eleven minus fifteen is minus four. So, ten to the minus four. A negative exponent means a fraction, here one ten-thousandth of a second, or a tenth of a millisecond.
beats.show: Ladder, right: '= 10⁽¹¹⁻¹⁵⁾'; on 'minus four', the exponent computes in place to '= 10⁻⁴ seconds'. On 'a fraction', a side note: '10⁻⁴ = 1 / 10,000'. On 'one ten-thousandth of a second', '= 0.0001 seconds' writes on with the 1 in the fourth decimal place highlighted. On 'a tenth of a millisecond', the decimal point hops three places right and the last line writes on, '= 0.1 milliseconds', boxed in amber.

beats.say: The units cancel too. Operations, top and bottom, go. Per second means divided by a second. Divide by that, and the second flips back to the top. Seconds are left, as a duration should be.
beats.show: Tiles and ladder dim to 30%, except the boxed '0.1 milliseconds'. The unit words in the fraction brighten: 'operations' over 'operations per second'. On 'go', both 'operations' strike through and fade. On 'divided by a second', 'per second' rewrites as '1 / second'. On 'flips back to the top', that small fraction flips so 'second' rises to the top line, and everything resolves to one white word, 'seconds', with a teal check.

beats.say: Multiply instead, and you get operations squared per second. Not a duration, not anything, so something is wrong.
beats.show: The ladder slides off. Right third: a grey panel titled 'the wrong way' builds 'operations × operations per second', which merges into 'operations² per second'. On 'not a duration', a grey cross stamp lands on it; on 'something is wrong', the panel desaturates and shrinks slightly.

beats.say: This five-second check catches most errors in this subject. Use it on every claim from here on, including the ones made here.
beats.show: Everything shrinks into a row of three small cards: amber 'operations ÷ operations/s → seconds' with a teal check; grey 'operations × operations/s' with a cross; coral '140 GB ÷ 4.8 TB/s → 29.2 ms' with a teal check, the earlier memory division passing the same test. Above them a teal banner writes on: 'check the units'. On 'including the ones made here', a teal magnifier swings round to face the viewer.

scenes.name: the gap, as a ratio and as a percentage
scenes.visual: Two horizontal bars on one shared scale, both starting at x=300, where 1,500 px stands for 30 ms (50 px per millisecond). Top row, labelled 'arithmetic': an amber bar exactly 5 px long, tag '0.1 ms', with the small grey tag 'all the arithmetic, packed together' carried over from the timeline. Bottom row, labelled 'the budget': a white-outlined bar with a faint grey fill, 1,500 px, tag '30 ms'. From b4 the sliver drops into the budget bar and a percent ruler (0 to 100%, 15 px per percent) draws beneath it. A small 'ratio' card at the top left persists from b1 to the end. The idea: one gap, said first as a multiple and then as a share, drawn to scale both times.

beats.say: Now the gap as a ratio. Thirty milliseconds over zero point one is three hundred. The budget is three hundred times the arithmetic.
beats.show: Left labels write on, 'arithmetic' and 'the budget', with tags '0.1 ms' (amber) and '30 ms' (white). On 'is three hundred', an equation card writes on, centred under the lane: '30 ÷ 0.1 = 300'. On 'three hundred times', a white card lands at the top left: 'ratio: 300 ×'.

beats.say: Drawn to one scale, the arithmetic is a barely visible sliver. On arithmetic alone, the chip could make three hundred tokens in the time it takes to make one.
beats.show: On 'one scale', the budget bar sweeps from x=300 to x=1800 and the amber bar appears at exactly 5 px; a thin white pointer drops onto it with the tag 'drawn to scale'. On 'three hundred tokens', the 5 px sliver copies itself into the left end of the budget bar and repeats end to end while a counter above runs '1 … 300 tokens'; at 300 the bar is exactly filled. The copies fade, leaving the budget bar empty again.

beats.say: In words, a ratio is easy to nod along to. Drawn to scale, it is hard to shrug off.
beats.show: The equation card fades. Nothing else moves except the empty budget bar, which brightens slightly, so the 5 px against 1,500 px contrast is the whole frame.

beats.say: Turn the ratio upside down. Zero point one over thirty is about zero point zero zero three three. As a percentage, a fraction out of a hundred, that is a third of one percent.
beats.show: The 'drawn to scale' pointer fades. The amber sliver drops from the top row into the left end of the budget bar, its 'packed together' tag riding with it; the top lane vanishes and the 'arithmetic' label stays, pointing at the sliver. Above the bar: '0.1 ÷ 30 = 0.0033'. On 'a fraction out of a hundred', the percent ruler draws beneath, ticks every 10% from '0%' to '100%', and the equation extends: '× 100 = 0.33%'. On 'a third of one percent', the camera zooms into the first 1% of the ruler, 15 px, which splits into three equal parts; the sliver fills exactly one. The camera zooms back out and the grey part gets its label: 'everything that is not arithmetic, 99.67%'.

beats.say: Unrounded, the hundred and forty billion gives nearer half a percent, and two hundred times rather than three. The exact figure depends on the model and the chip. The power of ten does not.
beats.show: A small grey working card at the right: '1.4 × 10¹¹ ÷ 10¹⁵ = 0.14 ms'. A dashed amber ghost extends the sliver from 5 px to 7 px, with its own small tag '≈ 0.47% unrounded', and a dashed ghost '≈ 214 ×' appears beside the 'ratio: 300 ×' card. On 'the model and the chip', a chip icon and a model-file icon flank the working card. On 'the power of ten does not', a white bracket spans 0% to 1% of the ruler, labelled 'under 1% either way'; then the ghosts, the icons, the bracket and the working card fade, leaving the solid 5 px sliver, the equation ending '0.33%', and 'ratio: 300 ×'.

beats.say: Two ways of saying one thing, because a ratio and a percentage land differently on different people.
beats.show: The equation above the bar condenses into a card that slides in beside 'ratio: 300 ×', joined to it by an equals sign: 'percentage: 0.33%' in amber. Hold.

scenes.name: where the thirty milliseconds goes
scenes.visual: The thesis frame of the chapter. Top band: title 'Where the 30 milliseconds goes', with a stopwatch icon at the top left reading '30 ms'. Centre: one bar, 1,500 px from x=210 to x=1710, drawn to scale: a 5 px amber sliver at the left labelled 'arithmetic, under 1%' that keeps its small grey 'packed together' tag, and the remainder labelled 'something else, 99%', which starts grey and floods coral during the scene (coral is the film's colour for bytes and memory traffic, so the colour change is the clue). Small cards appear below the bar and leave. Nothing on screen joins the hardware numbers with an operator: the next chapter teaches that the token time is set by whichever resource runs out first, not by a sum.

beats.say: So here is where the thirty milliseconds goes. Under one percent of it is mathematics. The other ninety-nine percent is something else.
beats.show: The title writes on. The bar from the previous scene glides up to centre at full size, keeping its 5 px sliver and its 'packed together' tag; the ruler, the old labels and both cards fade. On 'under one percent', the label 'arithmetic, under 1%' appears above the sliver with a pointer line. On 'something else', 'something else, 99%' writes on, centred in the grey remainder.

beats.say: The chip is not slow, and the model is not badly written. And there is a clue. The thirty milliseconds came from dividing bytes by memory speed.
beats.show: Below the bar, two small cards: a chip icon 'not slow' and a model-file icon 'not badly written', each with a teal check; they fade. On 'a clue', the bottom band writes on in coral: 'bytes ÷ bytes per second', and beneath it '140 GB ÷ 4.8 TB/s = 29.2 ms'. On 'memory speed', the grey remainder floods coral from left to right.

beats.say: Next chapter, this coral part gets its name. By the film's end, you will predict it for any model on any chip, from the model's size and two numbers off the chip's specification sheet.
beats.show: A coral tag with an empty name box and a '?' settles on the coral part, sub-label 'named next chapter'. The bottom band clears. Three small cards slide in under the bar, evenly spaced, with nothing between them: blue 'model size', amber 'compute rate', coral 'memory speed'. A grey bracket under the last two reads 'chip spec sheet'. A thin brace over all three draws one arrow up to the stopwatch, labelled 'any model, any chip'.

beats.say: This bar is the thesis of everything that follows. Every idea from here on is an attempt to shrink the coral part.
beats.show: Everything clears except the title and the bar. Teal arrows press in from the right end against the coral part, which compresses by a few percent and holds; a teal label above it reads 'shrink this'. Hold this frame for two seconds.

checks.claim: Bench example: input 0.5 times weight 0.13 = 0.065 (one operation)
Bench example: running total 1.2 + 0.065 = 1.265 (a second operation)
Operations per token: 70 billion weights x 2 (one multiply, one add) = 140 billion
140 billion is 1.4 x 10^11, so 'about ten to the eleven' rounds down (log10 = 11.15)
Ten to the fifteen = a thousand x a million x a million
Linear-scale bars with 10^15 = 1,500 px: the trillion bar is 1.5 px ('about one and a half pixels')
Linear-scale bars: the billion bar would be 0.0015 px, invisible
Log-scale bars: 1,500 px for 15 zeros = 100 px per power of ten (300/600/900/1200/1500 px; 10^11 at 1,100 px)

CORRECTION: the atlas caption says the two numbers are 'four steps apart', but a step on its list is a factor of a thousand. 10^15 / 10^11 is four powers of ten, a factor of 10,000, and 10^11 is not on the list at all (it sits between billion and trillion). The film says 'four powers of ten apart, a factor of ten thousand'.
CORRECTION (storyboard): the atlas's 'logarithmic' bars are 3/15/60/150/340 px, not proportional to the exponent. The film draws a true log scale, length proportional to the number of zeros.
Road-trip analogy: 300 km / 100 km/h = 3 hours
A quadrillion a second is a trillion every millisecond
10^11 operations at a trillion per millisecond = 0.1 ms
Exponent subtraction: 11 - 15 = -4; eleven tile pairs cancel, four tens left on the bottom
Ten to the minus four is one ten-thousandth = 0.0001
0.0001 seconds = 0.1 milliseconds
Time left over after the arithmetic: 30 - 0.1 = 29.9 ms
Tokens of arithmetic that fit in the 29.9 ms left over: 299, 'about three hundred more'
The ratio: 30 / 0.1 = 300
Drawn to scale on a 1,500 px bar for 30 ms, the 0.1 ms sliver is 5 px; 300 slivers fill the bar
Everything that is not arithmetic: 100 - 0.33 = 99.67%
Percent ruler: 1% of 1,500 px = 15 px; the 5 px sliver is one third of it
Earlier division re-checked for units: 140 GB / 4.8 TB/s = 0.0292 s = 29.2 ms
CAVEAT made explicit: unrounded, 1.4 x 10^11 / 10^15 = 0.14 ms of arithmetic, 0.47% of 30 ms ('nearer half a percent'); the 0.1 ms and 0.33% use 10^11 rounded down. Still under 1%.
Same caveat against the exact 29.2 ms and the H100/H200 dense 16-bit rating of 989 TFLOP/s (not narrated): 0.1416 ms, 0.49%
Unrounded sliver on the 1,500 px bar: 0.14 ms -> 7 px
CORRECTION (storyboard): the atlas's 'gap drawn to scale' bar draws arithmetic at 4 of 560 px (0.71%), not to scale; the film draws it at the true 0.33%, 5 px of 1,500
One second of the chip holds ten thousand tokens' worth of arithmetic: 10^15 operations per second / 10^11 operations per token
Timeline geometry: 1,500 px for 30 ms is 50 px per millisecond, so the packed 0.1 ms block is 5 px
CAVEAT made explicit (reviewer): unrounded, the ratio becomes 30 / 0.14 = 214, 'about two hundred times rather than three'
Same ratio against the exact 29.2 ms and 989 TFLOP/s (not narrated): about 206, still 'about two hundred'
'The power of ten does not [change]': 0.33% and 0.47% are both 10^-3 as fractions; 300 and 214 are both 10^2
checks.python: import math; print(math.floor(math.log10(0.1/30)), math.floor(math.log10(0.14/30)), math.floor(math.log10(30/0.1)), math.floor(math.log10(30/0.14)))
